claims.text: Precisely synchronizing reduction of all metal precursors yields a homogeneous, single-phase noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticle.
Even a slight reduction delay that staggers nucleation initiates phase separation and uncontrolled morphology.
The initial material is a single-source mixed precursor containing at least five noble-metal salts.
Atomic mobility is limited during solid-state reduction of the mixed precursor.
Adjusting heating ramp rate or injection timing can produce near-simultaneous reduction of every metallic component.
The relevant synthesis regime is rapid, kinetically controlled reduction at relatively low peak temperature.
Free atomic mobility is minimal and thermodynamic equilibrium is not reached during synthesis.
Synchronized nucleation freezes in a random homogeneous alloy by precluding time-dependent elemental segregation.
A fast, controlled reduction causes nearly simultaneous nucleation of the constituent metals.
Nucleation synchrony overwhelms differences in reduction potentials and mixing enthalpies that otherwise promote phase separation.
Limited mobility opposes element-interaction preferences and prevents substantial subsequent atomic rearrangement.
The optimized rapid profile will produce uniform, well-alloyed, single-phase nanoparticles.
The optimized rapid profile will preserve high surface-atom exposure and controlled defect levels.
Slower or staggered processing will produce elemental segregation, compositional inhomogeneity, and irregular morphology.
The proposed mechanism should extend to low-temperature syntheses using similar solid, mixed precursors with limited atomic mobility.
The mechanism may not apply to high-temperature liquid-phase synthesis or post-synthesis annealing where diffusion or equilibrium thermodynamics dominates.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats near-simultaneous reduction and nucleation as governing or effectively necessary for five-element HEA formation, but cited record PMC10621632::web::027::conclusions reports that single-phase five-element HEA particles formed even though the elements were reduced consecutively. That record instead attributes the result primarily to stochastic mixing with more atom types under limited-mobility conditions.
